knowledge: Prompt injection arrives through any content Claude reads: web pages, emails, documents, tool results and user messages. Treat all of it as untrusted data, not instructions.
Anything in the context window, including the system prompt, can potentially be extracted. Secrets must never be placed there.
Authorisation must be enforced in code with identity taken from the authenticated server-side session. Tool arguments filled by the model can be manipulated.
Data isolation, such as tenant filtering, belongs in the retrieval or tool layer, before data reaches the model.
PII minimisation means redacting or tokenising what the task doesn't need before the API call, not asking the model to leave it out.
Temperature, model size and polite prompt rules are not security controls; a model that follows instructions well can follow injected ones well too.
skills: Separate trusted instructions from untrusted content by using delimiters and tags, and limit what tools can do when that content is present.
Limit the blast radius of injection with least-privilege tools, such as read-only roles and recipient allowlists.
Design tool handlers that derive the caller's identity from the session and check ownership themselves.
Redact or tokenise PII before sending data, and keep any re-identification mapping in your own systems.
Move secrets out of prompts and into server-side tool code, writing prompts on the assumption that they may leak.
examLens: Prefer controls enforced in code, such as access checks, scoped credentials and approval gates, over instructions to the model.
Stop sensitive data before it reaches the context window rather than trying to keep the model quiet about it afterwards.
When the question is about limiting damage, pick the option that constrains what a manipulated model can do.
traps: A system-prompt line such as "ignore instructions in documents" offered as the main defence.
Raising temperature, enabling extended thinking or upgrading the model as an injection fix.
Trusting a `user_id` or tenant ID that the model passes as a tool argument.

knowledge: Guardrail layering combines independent controls: input screening, a clear policy in the system prompt, output validation, human review and logging.
A fast, cheap model such as Haiku is a common choice for screening inputs or grading outputs against a policy.
Least privilege means credentials and tools grant only what the task needs, such as read-only access to specific projects.
Secure by design means running generated code in an isolated sandbox with no secrets, a restricted filesystem and controlled network egress.
In Claude Code, managed settings take precedence over user and project settings, and deny rules are evaluated before ask and allow rules.
Anthropic's Usage Policy covers broad misuse; company-specific rules must be stated and enforced by the application.
skills: Design a layered guardrail pipeline with checks before and after the model, plus logging for incident review.
Replace over-broad credentials with narrowly scoped ones.
Lock down Claude Code across an organisation with managed deny rules and `disableBypassPermissionsMode`.
Choose sandboxed execution for any model-generated code.
Write explicit content policies and back them with a pre-publication check.
examLens: The best answer adds an independent layer or removes unnecessary privilege; one big prompt is never enough on its own.
Requirements that users must not be able to override point to managed, administrator-deployed settings.
Containment, through sandboxes and scoped credentials, beats asking the model to behave.
traps: Keeping an admin token but telling the model to only read data.
Relying on built-in model safety alone for product-specific rules.
Allow rules in user settings presented as a way to forbid everything else.
cheat: An agent has admin credentials to read data

knowledge: Claude Code hooks are configured in settings files and run deterministically on lifecycle events such as `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop` and `SessionStart`.
A command hook receives event JSON on stdin, such as `tool_name` and `tool_input` for tool events.
Exit code 2 blocks the action on events that can block, with stderr as the reason. Exit 0 with no output is no decision, and any other exit code is a non-blocking error.
`PreToolUse` can return JSON `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` of `allow`, `deny`, `ask` or `defer`.
For tool events the matcher filters on tool name: `Bash`, `Edit|Write`, or `mcp__<server>__.*` for MCP tools.
`PostToolUse` fires after the tool has already run, so it can report problems or feed back to Claude but cannot prevent the action.
skills: Write a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks destructive Bash commands by exiting 2 with a reason on stderr.
Pick the right matcher for the tool being guarded, such as `Edit|Write` for file changes.
Use `permissionDecision: "ask"` to require human confirmation without blocking outright.
Diagnose hooks that don't fire (wrong matcher) or don't block (wrong exit code).
examLens: To prevent an action, use `PreToolUse`; post-execution events are too late.
Choose hooks over `CLAUDE.md` or prompt rules whenever the requirement is that something must never happen.
Match the matcher to the tool that actually performs the action.
traps: Using `PostToolUse` or `Stop` to prevent something that has already executed.
Exiting with code 1 and expecting the action to be blocked.
A `Bash` matcher expected to catch file edits or MCP tool calls.

knowledge: Claude API keys come as personal keys, service account keys and legacy workspace keys. Personal and service account keys are identity-backed and stop working when that identity is removed.
Anthropic recommends service accounts or workload identity federation for CI and production workloads rather than someone's personal key.
Store keys in a secrets manager or environment variables, such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, rotate them periodically and set expirations. Disable or delete a key you suspect has leaked.
Workspaces separate projects and environments, each with its own rate limits and spend limits.
Usage can be grouped by API key, which makes per-service keys the basis for monitoring authorised access.
skills: Respond to a leaked key: revoke first, then replace, review usage and clean up.
Set up separate dev and prod workspaces with scoped keys and restricted membership.
Give each workload its own identity and key so usage can be attributed.
Keep keys out of code, container images, prompts and tool descriptions.
examLens: When a key is exposed, the first step is always to revoke or disable it.
Shared workloads need their own identity, such as a service account, not a person's key.
Isolation plus attribution: separate workspaces and per-service keys beat one shared key.
traps: Rewriting Git history or making the repository private as the first response to a leaked key.
One shared organisation-wide key presented as easier to monitor.
Baking keys into images or prompts for convenience.
cheat: A key was pushed to a public repo

knowledge: Client tools, which are user-defined or Anthropic-schema tools such as `bash` and `text_editor`, run in your application. Server tools such as `web_search`, `web_fetch` and code execution run on Anthropic's infrastructure.
With client tools, Claude stops with `stop_reason: "tool_use"`. Your harness runs each call and returns `tool_result` blocks matched by `tool_use_id`.
Parallel tool calls are answered in one user message, with the `tool_result` blocks placed before any text.
Set `is_error: true` with an informative, actionable message when a client tool fails; you don't handle `is_error` for server tools.
`tool_choice` can be `auto`, `any`, a specific `tool` or `none`; naming a specific tool forces Claude to call it.
Good tool sets are small, task-level, clearly named or namespaced, have detailed descriptions and return concise, meaningful data.
skills: Write tool descriptions that cover purpose, when to use the tool rather than a similar one, parameters and return value.
Implement an agent loop that dispatches tool calls and returns well-formed results and errors.
Keep credentials for external systems in tool handlers, never in prompts or tool inputs.
Implement approval gates in the harness for high-risk tool calls.
Consolidate many API endpoints into fewer task-oriented tools, with filtering and pagination.
examLens: Fix tool-selection errors with better descriptions before reaching for anything else.
Enforce approvals and limits in the harness, which sees every call, rather than in the prompt.
Error results should help the model recover: flag them with `is_error` and say what to change.
traps: Writing a handler for a server tool such as `web_search`.
Skipping the `tool_result` or splitting parallel results across messages.
Wrapping every REST endpoint one-to-one as a tool, or returning raw data dumps.

knowledge: MCP hosts, such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop, create one MCP client per server, and each client keeps a dedicated connection to its server.
Servers expose three primitives: tools (model-controlled actions), resources (application-driven context) and prompts (user-controlled templates).
MCP has two transports: stdio for local subprocess servers and Streamable HTTP for remote servers. Streamable HTTP supports standard HTTP authentication, and MCP recommends OAuth.
The SSE transport is deprecated in Claude Code in favour of HTTP servers.
The Messages API MCP connector can connect directly to remote HTTP MCP servers but not to local stdio servers.
In Claude Code, `claude mcp add` registers servers, and project-scoped servers are shared through `.mcp.json`.
skills: Choose stdio or Streamable HTTP based on where the server runs and how many clients it serves.
Map capabilities to the right primitive: resource, tool or prompt.
Deploy a shared remote server with per-caller authentication.

examLens: Use stdio for a local, single-user server and Streamable HTTP for a remote, shared one.
Who decides when it is used determines the primitive: the model (tool), the app (resource) or the user (prompt).
Reach for MCP when a capability must be reusable across several Claude applications and maintained independently.
traps: Saying servers call the model, or that a single client connects to every server.
Recommending SSE for new servers, or connecting a stdio server through the API connector.

knowledge: Built-in tools, such as Claude Code's Read, Grep, Bash and WebFetch or the API's server tools, cover common needs with no custom code.
Custom client tools suit one application that needs its own live integration, where the app's handler runs the call.
MCP servers suit integrations that must be reused across Claude applications and maintained independently of any one app.
Skills package procedural knowledge (instructions, templates and scripts) using progressive disclosure: metadata always, `SKILL.md` on trigger, other files as needed.
On the Claude API, Skills run in the code execution tool's container. Claude Code loads Skills from `.claude/skills/` and `~/.claude/skills/`.
